parole.significato: The use of originally accusative forms of pronouns, adjectives, articles, etc., in the nominative.

parole.significato: A Dutch liqueur made of egg yolks, sugar and strong liquor, typically brandy.

parole.significato: A person from, or residing in, Amsterdam.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch Amsterdammer.

parole.significato: A measure of wine or spirit equal to 10 gallons; a barrel of this capacity.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Antwerp.

parole.significato: Hold fast! Cease! Stop! Desist!

parole.significato: A sweet almond dessert pastry that originated in the Netherlands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch banket.

parole.significato: Any of several small chickens, especially of a breed that is a miniature version of another breed.

parole.significato: A simple wind instrument, such as a kazoo or tin horn.

parole.significato: A primitive trombone having wide tubes.
parole.testo: From an extension of the word bazoo (“mouth, boastful talk”), which ultimately probably stems from Dutch bazuin (“trumpet”). In the finance sense first used by policymakers during the European debt crisis (2010).

parole.significato: To besiege; to surround with troops.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch belegeren and/or Middle Low German belēgeren; equivalent to be- + lair. Compare also German belagern, Danish belejre. The English spelling was perhaps influenced by unrelated league.

parole.significato: A narrow ledge or shelf, as along the top or bottom of a slope.
parole.testo: From Dutch berm (“strip of roadside grass, verge”), probably via French berme, from Middle Dutch barm, baerm, barem (“verge, bank”), from Old Dutch *barm, from Proto-West Germanic *barm, from Proto-Germanic *barmaz (“edge, border, seam”).

parole.significato: Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, and Saba; the Caribbean Netherlands.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch bijlander, equivalent to by- + lander. See also belandre.

parole.significato: The backwater portion of a stream or remnant of an old stream bed.
parole.testo: From Dutch binnen (“inside”) + kil (“creek, kill”).

parole.testo: Calque of Dutch bisschopswijn.

parole.significato: to bark

parole.significato: A large basket woven from oak splints.
parole.testo: From Dutch bakkie, bakje, or less likely bokaal (“bowl, cup”).

parole.significato: To behave in a manner similar to the on-screen characters portrayed by Humphrey Bogart.
parole.testo: From the Dutch surname Bogaert, derived from bogaard, contraction of boomgaard (“orchard”), from boom (“tree”) + gaard (“garden”). Doublet of Baumgart, Bangert, and Bungert, all from German.

parole.significato: An obnoxious, selfish and overbearing person; an attention hog.
parole.testo: From actor Humphrey Bogart, from Dutch surname Bogaard (“keeper of an orchard”), from boomgaard (“treegarden, orchard”), cognate to English boom (“piece of wood”)/beam + garden. parole.significato: Money, especially when acquired or spent illegally or improperly; swag.
parole.testo: From Dutch boedel. Doublet of bottle (dialectal term meaning building or house).

parole.significato: To extend, or push, with a boom or pole.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch boom (“tree; pole”). Doublet of beam.

parole.significato: A peasant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch boer (“peasant”). Doublet of bauer, Boer, and bower (“peasant, farmer”). parole.testo: From Dutch boerenkool (“kale”). See cole.

parole.significato: A Bushman of southern Africa.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch Bosjesman.

parole.significato: Take care; look out.
parole.testo: From Dutch pas op from Afrikaans.

parole.significato: Eggplant; aubergine.
parole.testo: From Surinamese Dutch boulanger, from French beringène, from Arabic بَاذِنْجَان (bāḏinjān), from Persian بادنجان (bâdenjân). Doublet of aubergine.

parole.significato: In the early settlements of New York State, USA, a farm or estate.

parole.significato: Synonym of bakfiets.

parole.significato: A Flemish sloop with a castle at each end.

parole.significato: An alcoholic liquor distilled from wine or fermented fruit juice.
parole.testo: Shortened form of brandywine, from Dutch brandewijn (“burnt wine”). Compare German Brantewein, Branntwein, Danish brændevin.

parole.significato: Brandy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch brandewijn. Doublet of brännvin.

parole.significato: A building where beer is produced.
parole.testo: From Dutch brouwerij (“brewery”), equivalent to brew + -ery. See also brewhouse.

parole.significato: A Brussels carpet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch Brussel. The metonymic meaning of Brussels as the European Union stems from the fact that the EU headquarters is based in Brussels.

parole.significato: The African perennial grass Cenchrus ciliaris.
parole.testo: Via Afrikaans, ultimately from Dutch buffel (“buffalo”).

parole.significato: A small boat used for carrying provisions to ships lying at anchor in a harbour.
parole.testo: From Dutch bomschuit (“small fishing boat”) + boat.

parole.significato: A unit of measurement for land area used in the Low Countries.

parole.significato: The mayor, or head magistrate, of a town in the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany and certain other countries.
parole.testo: Partial calque of Dutch burgemeester with master. Compare also boroughmaster.

parole.significato: A slice of buttered bread.
parole.testo: From butter + ham, a calque of Dutch boterham.

parole.testo: Unclear. Perhaps from Dutch *kabbassen, from Old French cabasser (“put into a basket”), from cabas. Alternatively, perhaps from an earlier word *carbage (“shred”), a potential variant of *garbage (“wheat straw”).

parole.significato: One who works at a till or receives payments.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch cassier or French caissier, from French caisse.

parole.significato: A hooded seal.

parole.testo: From Dutch klinkaerd, later klinker, from klinken (“to ring, resound”).

parole.significato: a gable or facade with a decorative bell-shape, characteristic of traditional Dutch architecture
parole.testo: Calque of Dutch klokgevel, with klok meaning both bell and clock in Dutch, and gevel meaning gable.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch klapmuts (“three-piece cap or bonnet, hat with ear-flaps, hooded seal”).

parole.significato: The sound of feet hitting the ground loudly.
parole.testo: Probably onomatopoeic or a variant of clump (“walk heavily and clumsily”), itself also onomatopoeic or perhaps from the notion of walking in clumps, from Dutch klomp (“clump, mass, wooden shoe”).

parole.significato: The game of ninepins.
parole.testo: From Dutch klossen (“to play at bowls”).

parole.significato: A narrow valley with steep sides.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch klove (now kloof). Doublet of kloof.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch kaketoe, borrowed from Malay kakaktua. Spelling influenced by cock.

parole.significato: A beverage made by infusing the beans of the coffee plant in hot water.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch koffie, from Italian caffè, from Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve), from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa). Doublet of café and caffè and cognate with the words for "coffee" in other major European languages, most of which are derived from the Turkish and Italian words.

parole.significato: A small café or restaurant typically selling light refreshments along with coffee-based drinks.
parole.testo: From coffee + shop. Sense 2 is from Dutch coffeeshop, a pseudo-anglicism of this term.

parole.significato: A salad of finely shredded raw cabbage and sometimes shredded carrots, dressed with mayonnaise (white slaw) or a vinaig…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch koolsla (mentioned in English as the Dutch name by at least in 1794), from kool (“cabbage”) + sla (“salad”).

parole.significato: To seize for military use.
parole.testo: First attested in the late 19th century. From Dutch commanderen (“to command”), partially through its descendant, Afrikaans kommandeer (“to command”). Ultimately from French commander, from Old French comander, from Latin commendare. Doublet of command.

parole.significato: commissioner
parole.testo: From Dutch commissaris.

parole.significato: A Coney Island hot dog.
parole.testo: From Dutch Konijneneiland, from konijn[en] (“rabbit[s]”) + eiland (“island”), literally “island of rabbits”; equivalent to cony + island.

parole.significato: A Dutch official who performs inspections or oversight; an inspector.
parole.testo: From Dutch controleur.

parole.significato: To send a cookie to (a user, computer, etc.).

parole.significato: A large shallow fermentation vessel that allows efficient cooling during the production of beer.
parole.testo: Calque of Dutch koelschip.

parole.significato: A short coat of coarse cloth.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Dutch kort (“short”) + pije (“a coarse cloth”).

parole.significato: A two- or three-masted sailing vessel formerly used for transporting cargo in the Baltic Sea.
parole.testo: Ultimately probably from Dutch/Middle Dutch. Related to Danish krejert, kraier.

parole.significato: A game played outdoors with bats and a ball between two teams of eleven, popular in England and many Commonwealth count…
parole.testo: Perhaps from a Flemish dialect of Dutch met de krik ketsen (“to chase a ball with a curved stick”).

parole.significato: A sea or lake voyage, especially one taken for pleasure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch kruisen (“cross, sail around”), from kruis (“cross”), from Middle Dutch cruce, from Latin crux.

parole.significato: A donut in the form of a twisted ring.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch kruller (“curler”), from krullen + -er.

parole.significato: A cabin, for the use of the captain, in the after part of a sailing ship under the poop deck.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps a contraction from Dutch kajuit (“cabin”).

parole.significato: A historic unit of currency of the Netherlands, equivalent to one-and-a-half guilders.
parole.testo: From Dutch daalder. Doublet of thaler and dollar.

parole.significato: The political ideology of Belgian priest Adolf Daens and his followers.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Dutch daensisme. By surface analysis, Daens + -ism. Named after Belgian priest and politician Adolf Daens.

parole.significato: A person or object meant to lure somebody into danger.
parole.testo: From Dutch de + kooi, literally "the cage". Possibly related to verb coy (which itself may have been influenced by decoy).

parole.significato: Defeatism.

parole.significato: Blue and white earthenware produced in Delft, Netherlands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch Delft. Piecewise doublet of delved.

parole.significato: A minister of the Dutch Reformed Church; a predikant.

parole.significato: To rule over or control arbitrarily or arrogantly; to tyrannize.
parole.testo: From Dutch domineren, from Middle French dominer.

parole.significato: An expression of exasperation.
parole.testo: From Donner (or Donder) and Blitzen (or Blixem), the last two reindeer of Santa Claus's, named from Dutch donder (“thunder”) and bliksem (“lightning”).

parole.significato: A strong, untwilled linen or cotton.
parole.testo: From Dutch doek (“cloth, fabric, canvas”), from Middle Dutch doec, from Old Dutch *dōc, from Proto-West Germanic *dōk, from Proto-Germanic *dōkaz (“cloth”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwōg-, *dwōk- (“cloth”). See also duck (cloth).

parole.significato: . A drink.
parole.testo: From Dutch dop, from Middle Dutch dop, dup, doppe, from Old Dutch *dopp, *dupp, from Proto-West Germanic *dupp, from Proto-Germanic *duppaz (“hollow, shell, bowl”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Dop (“shell, pod, bowl”), German Topf (“pot”).

parole.significato: Any viscous liquid or paste, such as a lubricant, used in preparing a surface.
parole.testo: From Dutch doop (“thick dipping sauce”), from Dutch dopen (“to dip”), from Middle Dutch dopen, from Old Dutch *dōpen, from Frankish *daupijan, from Proto-Germanic *daupijaną. “Doop” in the sense “narcotic drug” ultimately refers to viscous opium juice, the drug of choice of the ancient Greeks; “insi

parole.significato: An Anabaptist or Baptist.
parole.testo: From Dutch doper.

parole.significato: A coarse sort of damask, originally made at Tournai, Belgium, and used for hangings, carpets, etc.
parole.testo: Dutch Doornik (“Tournai”)

parole.significato: A village or small town; a town considered provincial.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch dorp, which see for more. Doublet of dorf and thorp, and possibly also of troop and troupe.

parole.significato: An inhabitant of Schenectady, New York.
parole.testo: From Dutch dorp (“village”) + -ian.

parole.significato: A drudge; a minion or servile worker.
parole.testo: From Dutch druil (“sluggard”). Compare droll.

parole.significato: The effect of a picture appearing within itself recursively, so that the inner picture contains another even smaller pi…
parole.testo: Droste + effect, from Dutch Droste, from German Droste. From the image used on Droste-brand cocoa powder, one of the main Dutch brands, of a nurse carrying a serving tray with a cup of hot chocolate and a box with the same image. parole.significato: A kind of strong brown beer, originally from Belgian Trappist monasteries.
parole.testo: From Dutch dubbel (“double”). Doublet of double.

parole.significato: A former Dutch coin, originally of silver, worth one tenth of a guilder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch dubbeltje.

parole.significato: A tightly-woven cotton or linen fabric, often used as sailcloth.
parole.testo: From Dutch doek, from Middle Dutch doeck, doec (“linen cloth”), from Old Dutch *dōc, from Proto-West Germanic *dōk, from Proto-Germanic *dōkaz (“cloth, rag”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwōg-, *dwōk-. Cognate with German Tuch (“cloth”), Swedish duk (“cloth, canvas”), Icelandic dúkur (“cloth, fabric”)

parole.significato: A structure used to catch wildfowl, consisting of a central pond and radiating water-filled arms.
parole.testo: The sense relating to the structure may be (partially) borrowed from or influenced by Dutch eendenkooi.

parole.significato: A kind of coarse woolen cloth, having a thick nap or frieze.
parole.testo: From Dutch duffel, named after Duffel, a town in Belgium, itself ultimately from Latin Dubrolocus, the first particle from Gaulish dubrum.

parole.significato: A stupid person.
parole.testo: From dumb + head or dumb + -head, calque of Dutch domkop through its early form dom cop. Compare German Dummkopf (“dumbhead”).

parole.significato: A horizontal timber (or steel) section used in the construction of a building.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch dwang, from Middle Dutch dwanc.

parole.significato: A cloth for wiping or cleaning.
parole.testo: From Dutch dweil (“floorcloth”).

parole.significato: An obscure and intentionally preposterous sport in which teams take turns to dance while avoiding a "dwile" (beer-soake…
parole.testo: Possibly from dwile or Dutch dweil (“floorcloth”) and English flong, an old past tense of fling. The first documented game took place in 1966, despite hoaxing claims of a 16th-century origin.

parole.significato: Synonym of aardwolf (“Proteles cristatus”).
parole.testo: Calque of Dutch aardwolf (South African; compare Afrikaans aardwolf); by surface analysis, earth + wolf.

parole.significato: An upright frame, typically on three legs, for displaying or supporting something, such as an artist's canvas.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch ezel (“donkey; easel”), from Middle Dutch esel (“donkey”), from Proto-West Germanic *asil, from Latin asellus (“young ass or small donkey”), diminutive of asinus (“ass, donkey”), ultimately from an unknown source in Asia Minor. Essentially, the stand that a painting is placed on

parole.significato: A native of the East; an Easterner.
parole.testo: Possibly modeled on Dutch oosterling. Compare sterling.

parole.significato: An eleven-word poem, successive lines containing one, two, three, four and one words.
parole.testo: From eleven + -ie, calque of Dutch elfje or German Elfchen.

parole.significato: To construct polders in order to drain land
parole.testo: From em- + polder, probably influenced by Dutch inpolderen.

parole.significato: Narrow.
parole.testo: Probably from Dutch eng (“narrow”), also compare Old English enge (“narrow”), from Proto-West Germanic *angī, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *anguz. parole.significato: A small inherited house-and-garden lot in a village or settlement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from obsolete Dutch erf (“hereditament, plot of land”). Doublet of erf above.

parole.significato: To cut into a surface with an acid or other corrosive substance in order to make a pattern. Best known as a technique f…
parole.testo: From Dutch etsen (“to etch”), from German ätzen (“to etch”), from Old High German azzon (“to cause to bite or feed”), from Proto-Germanic *atjaną, causative of *etaną (“to eat”) (whence also English eat).

parole.significato: A long wooden slat, with holes for cords, that holds up an awning.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch juffrouw (“young woman”).

parole.significato: To increase the liveliness of a horse by inserting an irritant, such as a piece of peeled raw ginger or a live eel, in…
parole.testo: From Dutch vegen (“to sweep, strike”), from Middle Dutch vēghen (“to cleanse”), from Old Dutch *fegōn (“to cleanse”), from Proto-West Germanic *faginōn, from Proto-Germanic *faginōną (“to decorate, make beautiful”), from Proto-Indo-European *pōḱ-, *pēḱ- (“to clean, to adorn”). Cognate with Danish fe

parole.significato: An unkempt, slatternly person.
parole.testo: Possibly from Dutch feeks, probably from vegen (“to sweep, strike”): see etymology of feague (verb) above. Compare Middle English vecke (“old woman”).

parole.significato: corn salad or mâche, Valerianella locusta, a plant whose leaves are used in salads.
parole.testo: From Dutch vette kost (“fat food”).

parole.significato: A form of pole vaulting where the objective is to jump across a ditch as far as possible, rather than overcome a height.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch fierljeppen, from West Frisian fierljeppe.

parole.significato: An event or a display where fireworks are set off.
parole.testo: From fire + work(s). The similarity with Dutch vuurwerk and German Feuerwerk, both “fireworks”, is hardly coincidental. parole.significato: To act clumsily or confused; to struggle or be flustered.
parole.testo: Possibly from the noun. Probably a blend of flounce + founder or a blend of founder + blunder or from Dutch flodderen (“wade”). See other terms beginning with fl, such as flutter, flitter, float, flap, flub, flip.

parole.significato: A heavy, coarse cloth manufactured from shoddy.
parole.testo: Named after the dated anglicized Dutch city name Flushing (“Vlissingen”) where the wool was made, from Dutch Vlissingen, further etymology is uncertain.

parole.significato: A kind of Dutch sailing vessel developed in the 16th century, used to transport cargo.
parole.testo: From Dutch fluyt, archaic spelling of fluit. Doublet of flauta and flute.

parole.significato: A large flat-bottomed coasting vessel, formerly found in Holland, Spain and Portugal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch vlieboot, but re-analysed as fly + boat.

parole.significato: A very large wooden vat in which beer is lagered.
parole.testo: From Dutch foeder, voeder; from Old Dutch *fuodar, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą. Doublet of fother and fodder.

parole.significato: To introduce or insert surreptitiously or without warrant.
parole.testo: Probably from archaic Dutch vuisten (“to take into one’s hand”), from Middle Dutch vuysten, from vuyst (“fist”); akin to Old English fyst (“fist”).

parole.significato: Any of a class of aeroplanes produced by the Fokker company, used by Germany in World War I.
parole.testo: From Dutch Fokker * (aeroplanes): From the company name, Fokker, after its founder, Anthony Fokker.

parole.significato: A juvenile locust or grasshopper while in its wingless or flightless phase.
parole.testo: Perhaps from Dutch or Afrikaans voetganger (“pedestrian”, literally “foot-goer”), or a partial calque of German Fußgänger (“pedestrian”), equivalent to foot + ganger (“goer, walker, stepper”).

parole.significato: An adventurer who pillages, plunders, or thieves privately or for compensation; or wages ad-hoc war on other nations, s…
parole.testo: From free + booty + -er. Calque of Dutch vrijbuiter (literally “free booty-er”), from vrij (“free”) + buit (“booty”) + -er (occupational suffix). Doublet of filibuster.

parole.significato: A Dutch condiment resembling sweetened mayonnaise, often served on French fries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch fritessaus, from frites (“French fries”) + saus (“sauce”).

parole.significato: Merry, joyous, full of mirth; later especially, frolicsome, sportive, full of playful mischief.
parole.testo: From Dutch vrolijk (“cheerful”), from Middle Dutch vrolijc, from Old Dutch frōlīk, from Proto-Germanic *frawalīkaz. Compare German fröhlich (“blitheful, gaily, happy, merry”). parole.significato: Mental depression.
parole.testo: 1743, Scottish and Northern English dialectal word, originally a verb meaning “to panic, fail due to panic”. Perhaps from or cognate with obsolete Dutch fonck (“distress, agitation”), from Middle Dutch fonck (“perturbation, agitation”). More at flunk.

parole.significato: A leave of absence or vacation.
parole.testo: From Dutch verlof (“furlough”), probably from Middle Low German verlōf (“furlough, permission”) (possibly via German Verlaub), from the verb verlōven (“to allow”), from Old Saxon far- + lōvian (“to trust, believe”). From Middle Low German also German Verlaub, Danish forlov. Doublet of leave.

parole.significato: A type of fish-trap consisting of tubular nets that are supported by hoops.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch fuik (“fish trap”), from Middle Dutch vuyke, fuke. Cognate with West Frisian fûke, German Low German Fuuk.

parole.significato: A subgenre of hardcore techno characterised by an intense, distorted kick sound and controversial lyrics or samples.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch gabber (literally “friend”), from Yiddish חבֿר (khaver). Doublet of chaver.

parole.significato: The board on a boat which attaches to the keel running fore and aft along the bottom.
parole.testo: From Dutch gaarboord, equivalent to gather + board.

parole.significato: Matter in an intermediate state between liquid and plasma that can be contained only if it is fully surrounded by a sol…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch gas, coined by chemist Jan Baptist van Helmont in Ortus Medicinae. Derived from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos, “chasm, void, empty space”); perhaps also inspired by geest (“breath, vapour, spirit”). Doublet of chaos. First attested in 1648.

parole.significato: An inshore channel or strait dividing two landmasses (such as two islands or sandbanks, or an island and a peninsula, e…
parole.testo: From Dutch gat and/or Middle Low German gat. Compare Icelandic gat.

parole.significato: Any lizard in the infraorder Gekkota.
parole.testo: The modern form was probably borrowed into English and other European languages from Dutch gekko (1718). Contemporary English forms were chacco (1711) and jackoa (1724). parole.significato: Gin, especially jenever.
parole.testo: An alteration of Dutch genever under the influence of the geonym Geneva.

parole.significato: Having a cosy or pleasant, or sociable atmosphere; convivial and inviting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch gezellig, from Middle Dutch gesellich, from geselle (“companion”) + -ich (suffix forming adjectives). parole.significato: A small cucumber, often pickled whole.
parole.testo: From a form of Dutch gurk, an archaic variant of augurk (“small pickled cucumber”), from Low German, from Middle Low German agurke, augurke, probably via Slavic (compare Polish ogórek), from Byzantine Greek ἀγγούριον (angoúrion, “cucumber”). parole.significato: To laugh gently in a playful, nervous, or affected manner.
parole.testo: Early 16th century, probably of imitative origin. Or, perhaps a frequentative based on dialectal English gig (“to creak”), from Middle English gigen (“to make a creaking sound”) + -le; or perhaps of Dutch or Low German origin: compare Saterland Frisian güüchelje (“to giggle”), West Frisian giechelje

parole.significato: Someone connected with Gillingham Football Club, as a fan, player, coach etc.
parole.testo: * As an English surname, converged from variants of Giles (sometimes through Dutch), Julian, and William. * As a northern English surname, from Middle English gil (“ravine, glen”), from Old Norse gil. parole.significato: A colourless non-aged alcoholic liquor made by distilling fermented grains such as barley, corn, oats or rye with junip…
parole.testo: Abbreviation of geneva, alteration of Dutch genever (“juniper”) from Old French genevre (modern French genièvre), from Vulgar Latin ziniperus, from Latin iūniperus (“juniper”). Hence gin rummy (first attested 1941).

parole.significato: A large antelope of the genus Connochaetes, native to Africa, having curved horns.
parole.testo: From Dutch gnoe, from Khoekhoe ǃnu:, of unknown origin, likely onomatopoeic of the grunt-type noise of the gnu.

parole.significato: A little god; a minor or inferior deity; godling.
parole.testo: From god + -kin, perhaps also from Dutch godeken (“godkin”).

parole.significato: A follower of Franciscus Gomarus, a 17th-century Dutch Calvinist who strongly opposed the Arminians; an adherent of ort…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch gomarist.

parole.testo: From Goropius + -ism (suffix forming names of schools of thought, systems, or theories), possibly influenced by French goropiser (“to goropize”), coined by the German philosopher and scientist Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) in his work Nouveaux essais sur l’entendement humain (New Essays on H

parole.significato: A type of semi-hard to hard cheese originating in the Netherlands.
parole.testo: From the Dutch city of Gouda.

parole.significato: A female ruler or regent.
parole.testo: From Dutch gouvernante, and its source, Middle French gouvernante. Compare govern.

parole.significato: A Dutch earl or count.
parole.testo: From Dutch graaf. Doublet of graf and grave.

parole.significato: A canal in a city, with houses on each side.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch gracht.

parole.significato: having a rough, surly, and harsh demeanor and nature.

parole.significato: An herbal mixture, used in the flavouring of beer, that preceded the use of hops.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch gruit. Doublet of grit.

parole.significato: To shift a fore-and-aft sail from one side of a sailing vessel to the other, while sailing before the wind.
parole.testo: Probably from Dutch gijben (obsolete), gijpen; cognate with Danish gibbe, German gieben, giepen, Swedish gipa, gippa. The noun is derived from the verb; compare Dutch gijb (obsolete), gijp (“act of gybing; a boom”).

parole.significato: The amount of beer brewed at a time.
parole.testo: From Dutch gijl, from gijlen (“to ferment”).

parole.significato: cod salted and dried.
parole.testo: From Dutch abberdaan, labberdaan, or a French [Term?] form. Compare Old French habordeau, from the name of a Basque district, and French Labourd, adjective Labourdin. The letter l was misunderstood as the French article l'.

parole.significato: Small, oblong, sweet-tasting chocolate granules, which are sprinkled on slices of buttered bread or rusks.
parole.testo: From Dutch hagelslag.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of The Hague.
parole.testo: From Dutch Hagenaar.

parole.significato: A form of reduced-fat margarine from Holland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch halvarine.

parole.significato: The cloth that covers a coachbox.
parole.testo: Probably from Dutch hemel (“heaven, canopy, tester”) (akin to German Himmel, and perhaps also to English heaven) + cloth; or perhaps a corruption of hamper cloth.

parole.significato: An unborn child.
parole.testo: From Dutch Hans in kelder (“Hans in the cellar”).

parole.significato: A shark (cartilaginous fish of Selachimorpha).
parole.testo: From Dutch haai (“shark”) or West Flemish haaie (formerly haeye), from the Old Norse hái, a short form of hákarl (“shark”) (a compound of há- (“marks fish of the shark kind”) + karl (“a man”)). The German Hai, the Swedish haj and the Danish haj are from the same source.

parole.significato: A terrine made from the flesh of the head of a pig (such as the face).
parole.testo: Calque of Dutch hoofdkaas.

parole.significato: Synonym of tadpole person.
parole.testo: From head + foot + -er. Possibly a calque of Dutch kopvoeter / koppoter, and/or of German Kopffüßler.

parole.significato: An open-air religious service held by Calvinists in the Low Countries during the Reformation, typically in rural areas…
parole.testo: Calque of Dutch hagenpreek, from hage (“hedge”) + preek (“sermon”).

parole.significato: In Holland, and, until the 19th century, also in Cape Colony, a council to assist a local magistrate in the government…
parole.testo: From Dutch heemraad (“village council”).

parole.significato: A Dutch lord.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch heer.

parole.significato: An annual herb, of species Lamium amplexicaule, with pink or purple flowers and deeply crenate leaves.
parole.testo: Calque of Dutch hoenderbeet. By surface analysis, hen + bit (past participle of bite; bitten). First attested in 1578. parole.significato: To leave with a pawnbroker as security for a loan.
parole.testo: From the phrase in hock, circa 1855-60, from Dutch hok (“hutch, hovel, jail, pen, doghouse”). Compare also Middle English hukken (“to sell; peddle; sell at auction”), see huck.

parole.significato: A kind of strong alcoholic drink.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch hoogmogenden or hoogmogendheden (“eminence”, title of members of the States General).

parole.significato: A painting by William Hogarth.
parole.testo: Of Dutch origin, hoog (“high”) + aard (“nature or character”).

parole.significato: A Dutch polytechnic or college; a higher education institution of lower rank than a university.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch hogeschool.

parole.significato: A case for carrying a tool, particularly a gun, safely and accessibly.
parole.testo: From Dutch holster (“pistol-case, holster”), from Middle Low German holster, from Old Saxon *holster, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hulastrą, *hulistrą (“hull, case, covering”). parole.significato: A small fishing boat.
parole.testo: From Dutch hoeker, an alteration of Middle Dutch hoecboot, from hoec + boot.

parole.significato: Absence from school or work; truancy.
parole.testo: First attested in 1848 in New York City. Most likely from Dutch hoekje (“nook, corner; 'spot to hide' in hide-and-seek”). Formerly, "hoekje spelen" could be used to mean "to play hide-and-seek", though the common term for the game nowadays is verstoppertje. By surface analysis, hook + -y.

parole.significato: Horrible to hear.
parole.testo: From Dutch horribile auditu, from Latin horribile audītū (literally “horrible to hear”).

parole.significato: A member of the Khoekhoe group of peoples.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch Hottentot, its first known use in Dutch being in the 1650s. parole.significato: A cannon that combines certain characteristics of field guns and mortars, delivering projectiles with medium velocities…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch houwitser, from German Haubitze, from Middle High German haufniz, from Czech houfnice, which was derived from houf (“flock, crowd”) + -nice. The Czech noun houf comes from Middle High German hufe (“heap”), from Old High German hūfo.

parole.significato: Hello; what's up?
parole.testo: Contraction of how is it? In South Africa, possibly a calque of Flemish Dutch hoe is 't?.

parole.significato: Hey! ho!, hallo!, stop!
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch hoi, compare ahoy.

parole.significato: A mound of earth.
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Dutch homp (“hump, lump”) or Middle Low German hump (“heap, hill, stump”), from Old Saxon *hump (“hill, heap, thick piece”), from Proto-Germanic *humpaz (“hip, height”), from Proto-Indo-European *kumb- (“curved”). parole.significato: A goal or base in children's games.
parole.testo: From Dutch honk (“the base in a game”).

parole.significato: To push someone roughly; to crowd; to jostle.
parole.testo: From Dutch husselen or by metathesis from Dutch hutselen (“to shake up”), a frequentative of hutsen (“to stir, to move something (back and forth)”).

parole.significato: The seaward end of a glacier.
parole.testo: Partial calque of Dutch ijsberg (compound of ijs (“ice”) + berg (“mountain”)), from Middle Dutch ijsberch. parole.significato: An unspecified belief in an undefined transcendent reality.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch ietsisme. By surface analysis, Dutch iets (“something”) + English -ism.

parole.significato: A soft cookie baked on a checkered iron plate that gives it a characteristic pattern.
parole.testo: From Dutch ijzerkoekje.

parole.significato: Having been pawned.
parole.testo: From Dutch hok (“hutch, hovel, jail, pen, doghouse”).

parole.significato: A Eurasian person living in or connected with Indonesia, especially (historical) a person in the former Dutch East Indi…
parole.testo: Clipping of Indo-European or Indonesia; from Dutch Indo.

parole.significato: A form of gelatin obtained from the air bladder of the sturgeon and certain other fish, used as an adhesive and as a cl…
parole.testo: Apparently from obsolete Dutch huisenblas, from German Hausenblase, from Hausen (“sturgeon of the Huso genus”) + Blase (“bladder”), with alteration after glass.

parole.significato: A Dutch and Flemish alcoholic spirit, flavoured with juniper, rather like gin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch jenever (“jenever”), from Old French genevre, from Vulgar Latin ziniperus, from Latin iūniperus (“juniper”).

parole.significato: To shift, or swing around, as a sail, boom, yard, etc., as in tacking.
parole.testo: Attested since the 1680s (also spelled jibe and gybe), perhaps from Dutch gijben (a variant of gijpen (“to turn sails suddenly”), whence certainly the form jibe) or else from Danish gibbe (“jib, jibe”), related to Swedish gippa (“jib, jibe, jerk, make jump”). Compare also Middle High German gempeln

parole.significato: legal, juridical, pertaining to the law and jurisprudence
parole.testo: Calque of obsolete Dutch juristisch.

parole.significato: A tiny folkloric man who traditionally wears a pointy red hat, lives in harmony with nature and resides in mushrooms, s…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch kabouter (“gnome”).

parole.significato: Synonym of sakabula.
parole.testo: Following a common pattern of naming South African flora and fauna kaffir (originally a neutral term for Bantu, now offensive) followed by an analogous European plant or animal. The compounding may have happened in English or Afrikaans; the components derive from Dutch kaffer and vink.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Kangean, its inhabitants, or their language or culture.
parole.testo: From Kangean + -ese, from Dutch Kangeanisch or Kangeansch, from Kangean kangean or kangayan.

parole.significato: A German industrial cartel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch kartel.

parole.testo: From Dutch ranten, randen (“to talk nonsense, rave”), from Middle Dutch ranten (“to rant, babble, goof around”), of uncertain origin; but apparently related to Middle High German ranzen (“to dance, jump around, frolic”), German ranzen (“to be ardent, be in heat, copulate, mate, ramble, join up”).

parole.significato: To entwine or tangle (something) confusedly; to entangle.
parole.testo: The verb is borrowed from Dutch ravelen, rafelen (“to tangle, become entangled; to fray; to unweave”) [and other forms]; further etymology uncertain. parole.significato: An obsolete currency in Curaçao, equivalent to six stuivers.
parole.testo: From Dutch reaal, from Spanish real. Doublet of royal.

parole.significato: To pass (a rope) through a hole or opening, especially so as to fasten it.
parole.testo: Apparent alternative form of reef (“to pull or yank strongly”, verb) or from Dutch reven (“to take in, insert”).

parole.significato: A member of the Dutch Arminians whose divergence from Calvinism was expressed in five articles in the Remonstrance of 1…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch remonstrant, from Latin remōnstrāns.

parole.significato: A strip of worked leather, especially as used to form crisscrossed patterns on the back of chairs etc.
parole.testo: From South African Dutch riempje, later Afrikaans riempie, diminutive form of riem.

parole.significato: A Dutch coin worth 2+¹⁄₂ guilders.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch rijksdaalder.

parole.significato: a national heritage site of the Netherlands
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch rijksmonument (“state monument”).

parole.significato: A large meal originating in colonial Indonesia composed of many different dishes with rice as the main ingredient; seve…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch rijsttafel (“rice table”).

parole.significato: A silver coin and money of account in use from the late-16ᵗʰ to the mid-19ᵗʰ centuries in the European Teutonic countri…
parole.testo: Borrowed from obsolete Dutch rijcksdaler (modern rijksdaalder), after early modern German Reichsthaler.

parole.significato: An obsolete currency used in much of continental Europe, as well as some Dutch colonies (even after they had become Bri…
parole.testo: From obsolete forms of Dutch rijksdaalder.

parole.significato: A traditional Malaysian and Indonesian salad of mixed raw fruits and vegetables served with a sauce.
parole.testo: From Dutch roedjak, from Javanese ꦫꦸꦗꦏ꧀ (rujak), from Old Javanese rujak.

parole.significato: A kind of sausage, made in a bag of tripe, sliced and fried, famous among the Dutch of New Amsterdam.
parole.testo: Dutch rolletje (“a little roll”).

parole.significato: A list of individuals or groups, usually for an organization of some kind such as military officers and enlisted person…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch rooster (“gridiron, table, list”), from Middle Dutch roosten (“to roast”). More at roast.

parole.significato: A small alcid of the north Atlantic, the little auk, Alle alle.
parole.testo: Probably from Dutch rotje (“petrel”).

parole.significato: A circular prison, especially a small local lockup or station house.
parole.testo: From round + house, a calque of Dutch rondhuis (“guardhouse”). First attested in the Mid-15th c.

parole.significato: A large drinking-glass for alcoholic drinks, chiefly wine, typically with a short or heavy stem.
parole.testo: Partly from Dutch roemer, rummer (West Flanders); partly from Middle Low German römer; partly from German Römer (“Roman person or thing”), named because it was made in glassworks dating from the Roman era. See also roemer; and for the etymology compare Romeware.

parole.significato: A mounted warrior, or knight
parole.testo: From Dutch ruiter, from Middle Dutch ruter, from Old French routier.

parole.significato: A gold coin of Zealand (Netherlands) worth 14 florins.
parole.testo: From Dutch rijder, properly, a rider.

parole.significato: Synonym of sagueir (palm wine made from Arenga pinnata).
parole.testo: From Dutch sagoweer, from Portuguese sagueiro, ultimately from Malay sagu (“sago”); compare Makasar sagéru, Buginese sagéru, Malay saguer, Malay sageru. Doublet of sagwire.

parole.significato: A sluice or lock, as in a river or canal, to make it more navigable.
parole.testo: Dutch sas, from French sas (“the basin of a waterfall”).

parole.significato: A framework for holding wood so that it can be sawed; a sawhorse.
parole.testo: * From saw + buck, calque of Dutch zaagbok. * (ten-dollar bill): From the resemblance of the Roman numeral X (ten) to a sawhorse.

parole.significato: A quick, light run.
parole.testo: First attested in 1687. Origin uncertain, but possibly from Dutch schamperen, from Old French escamper, from Vulgar Latin *excampāre.

parole.significato: A member of an Eastern Woodlands tribe descended from an association of Mahican, Potatuck, Weantinock, Tunxis, and Podu…
parole.testo: A Dutch-influenced form of the R-dialect Algonquian Pishgachtigok (“gathered waters, confluence”).

parole.significato: A silver coin formerly current in the Low Countries.
parole.testo: From Dutch schelling.

parole.significato: A villain or scoundrel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch schelm.

parole.significato: An old Dutch measure of volume used for wheat, etc.
parole.testo: From Dutch schepel.

parole.significato: A Dutch magistrate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch schepen.

parole.significato: A small breed of dog developed in Belgium, sometimes used as a watchdog on boats.
parole.testo: From Belgian Dutch (Flemish), but unclear at the word level. * Conventionally taken to be schipper (“skipper”) + -ke (“diminutive suffix”), allegedly alluding to a role as watchdog and/or rodent catcher on canal boats. * Alternatively, a mutation of scheperke, a diminutive of scheper (“shepherd, she

parole.significato: A municipal officer in the North American Dutch colonies.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch schout.

parole.significato: A flat-bottomed Dutch river-boat; a barge.
parole.testo: From Dutch schuit. Compare shout ("flat-bottomed boat"), scout (“swift sailing boat”).

parole.significato: A large flat-bottomed boat, having broad, square ends.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch schouw.

parole.significato: To scratch (something) with claws or fingernails; to claw.
parole.testo: The verb is a variant of dialectal English scramb (“to pull or rake together with the hands; to gather a handful of something from the ground; to scratch with the claws or nails; to pull down violently; to tear off; to maul about; a handful of something from the ground”), possibly related to Dutch s

parole.significato: To scratch (something) with claws or fingernails; to claw, to scram.
parole.testo: The verb, especially sense 2 (“to scratch with the claws or fingernails”), is possibly related to Dutch schrammen (“to graze, scratch”) and German schrammen (“to scratch, scrape”), from Late Middle High German schramm, schramme (“a graze, scratch”); further etymology unknown. parole.significato: To grind with the teeth, and with a crackling sound; to crunch.
parole.testo: Compare Dutch schransen (“to eat greedily”), German schranzen. Compare crunch, scrunch.

parole.significato: To tear or scratch.
parole.testo: Probably from Dutch schrammen, from schram (“a rent, a tear”).

parole.significato: To card or tease (wool) coarsely; to run through a scribbler.
parole.testo: From Dutch schribbelen (“to scratch”), from Middle Dutch schrobben (“to scrub, scrape, scratch”), variant of schrapen, schrappen. Related to scrub.

parole.significato: A type of hoe, manipulated by both pushing and pulling, with a sharp blade parallel with the worked surface; an instanc…
parole.testo: The noun is a borrowing from Dutch schoffel; the English verb arose via subsequent verbification within English but is also parallel with Dutch schoffelen.

parole.significato: A swing.
parole.testo: From Dutch schop.

parole.significato: The edge of a woven fabric, where the weft (side-to-side) threads run around the warp (top to bottom) threads, creating…
parole.testo: From early modern Dutch selfegghe (Modern Dutch zelfkant (“selvage”)), equivalent to self + edge.

parole.significato: A member of a tribe of Native Americans in western New York state.
parole.testo: From Dutch Sennecaas, from Algonquian (probably Mahican [Term?]).

parole.significato: A short line added to the end of a stroke in traditional typefaces, such as Times New Roman.
parole.testo: From earlier ceriph, seriph, surryph, of obscure derivation. parole.significato: The curve of the main deck or gunwale from bow to stern.
parole.testo: Perhaps from Dutch scheren (“to move aside, skim”); see also shear.

parole.significato: To move along a surface (ice or ground) using skates.
parole.testo: Back-formation from Dutch schaats, from Middle Dutch schāetse, from Old Northern French escache (“a stilt, trestle”) (compare French échasse and English scatch), from a Germanic language, perhaps Frankish *skakkjā (“stilt”, literally “thing that moves”), related to *skakan (“to shake, swing”).

parole.significato: A thin strip of an osier (“long, pliable twig from a plant, usually a willow”) used in basketmaking.
parole.testo: From Dutch scheen (“strip of metal or wood; (anatomy) shin”), from Middle Dutch schene, from Old Dutch *skina, from Proto-West Germanic *skinu (“bar; track; (anatomy) shin; spine”), from Proto-Germanic *skinō (“piece; plate; rim; (anatomy) shinbone”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *skey- (“to di

parole.significato: To make a brief, basic drawing.
parole.testo: From Dutch schets or German Skizze, from Italian schizzo, from Latin schedium, from Ancient Greek σχέδιος (skhédios, “made suddenly, off-hand”), from σχεδόν (skhedón, “near, nearby”), from ἔχω (ékhō, “to hold”). Compare scheme.

parole.significato: An umbelliferous plant (Sium sisarum), cultivated for its sweet edible tuberous roots.
parole.testo: From Dutch suikerwortel (literally “sugar-root”).

parole.significato: A rotating iron disk coated with oil and diamond dust used to polish the facets of a diamond.
parole.testo: Probably from Dutch schijf (“slice”), probably influenced by shive. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skībǭ (“a shaving; slice”). Cognate to English shive, German Scheibe (“slice”), Old Norse skífa (“to cut into slices, slice”).

parole.significato: One who uses a skive (or skives).
parole.testo: From skive (“to shave”) + -er. Probably from Dutch schijf (“slice”), probably influenced by shive.

parole.significato: Slaw.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch sla, shortened from salade (“salad, lettuce”). See also slaw.

parole.significato: Coleslaw.
parole.testo: Borrowed (around 1861) from Dutch sla, shortened from salade (“salad, lettuce”).

parole.significato: A low sled drawn by animals, typically on snow, ice or grass.
parole.testo: Dialectal Dutch sleedse, from Middle Dutch sleedse, from the root of sled.

parole.significato: A vehicle, generally pulled by an animal, which moves over snow or ice on runners, used for transporting persons or goo…
parole.testo: From Modern Dutch slee, from Middle Dutch slede, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *slidô. Doublet of sled and further related to slide.

parole.significato: A frozen pond on which people skate.
parole.testo: One suggestion is that the term in its meaning of "children's slide" derives from the literal meaning by extension. Another is that it derives from Dutch glijbaan or the earlier form glijd-baene: note the common pronunciation of pond in sliding pond as /pɑn/.

parole.significato: A single-masted sailboat with only one headsail.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch sloep. Doublet of chalupa and shallop.

parole.motivo_incerta: or from; either; modificatore <unc> nel legame
parole.significato: To import or export, illicitly or by stealth, without paying lawful customs charges or duties
parole.testo: From earlier smuckle, either from Dutch smokkelen (“to smuggle”), a frequentative form of Middle Dutch smūken (“to act secretly, be sneaky”), from Old Dutch *smugan, or from Dutch Low Saxon or German Low German smuggeln; all are from Proto-West Germanic *smeugan (“to creep; slip through or into”). c

parole.significato: A broad-mouthed, loose-ringed bit (metal in a horse's mouth). It brings pressure to bear on the tongue and the corners…
parole.testo: Apparently from Dutch snavel, from Middle Dutch snavel, snabel (“snout”), diminutive of Middle Dutch snabbe, snebbe (“bird's bill, neb”). Akin to Old Frisian snavel (“mouth”), Middle Low German snabbe (“neb, beak”), Old English nebb (“beak, bill, nose, face”). More at neb.

parole.significato: A flintlock.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch snaphaan.

parole.significato: To cut or thrust while fighting with a knife; to use a knife as a weapon.
parole.testo: From Dutch steken of snijden (literally “to stab or cut”). The initial st- later assimilated to the sn- of snick.

parole.significato: A cookie in which the batter is rolled into a ball and coated with cinnamon sugar.
parole.testo: The earliest known use is from 1889. Possibly a fanciful coinage, from snicker + doodle (“doodlebug”; though without clear semantic connection to either word). parole.significato: To cut with short sharp actions, as with scissors.
parole.testo: From Dutch snippen (“to snip; shred”) or Low German snippen (“to snip; shred”), of imitative origin. Compare snap.

parole.significato: controlled multisensory stimulation, a type of therapy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch snoezelen.

parole.significato: A freshwater and marine fish of the family Centropomidae in the order Perciformes.
parole.testo: From Dutch snoek (“pike, Esox”). Doublet of snoek; perhaps more distantly related to snake.

parole.significato: To be devious and cunning so as not to be seen.
parole.testo: From Dutch snoepen (“to pry, eat in secret, sneak”) or maybe Old Norse snópa (“to idle about dismally”), or (“to use a blood found”). Related to Dutch and Low German snappen (“to bite, seize”), Dutch snavel (“beak, bill, pecker, neb”), German Schnabel (“beak, bill, mouth”). More at snap.

parole.significato: To snore.
parole.testo: From Dutch snorken or Middle Low German snorken, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *fnoʀukōn (“to snore, snort”).

parole.significato: A square-rigged sailing vessel similar to a brig formerly used as a warship, with a foremast, a mainmast, and a trysail…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch snauw, snaauw, or Low German snau; further etymology uncertain, possibly from Low German snau (“beak”), related to Middle Low German snute (“snout”) (whence English snout), from Proto-West Germanic *snūt (“snout”), from Proto-Germanic *snūtaz (“snout”), possibly imitative.

parole.significato: A mouse-like creature which, according to folklore, Dutch women who sit over stoves give birth to.
parole.testo: From dialectal Dutch zoeterke(n) (“sweatheart”) (compare zoetje, zoetke (“sweetheart”)), equivalent to sweet + -kin or soot + -kin.

parole.significato: A common East Asian liquid sauce, made by subjecting boiled beans to long fermentation and then long digestion in salt…
parole.testo: 1670s; borrowed from Dutch soja, from the Satsuma pronunciation of Japanese 醤油 (soi), variant of the standard Japanese 醤油 (shōyu). Doublet of shoyu, orthographic borrowing from Middle Chinese 醬油 (tsjàng-yuw), from 醬 (tsjangᴴ, “bean paste”) + 油 (“oil”).

parole.significato: a rope or fetter used to hobble a horse or other animal
parole.testo: From Dutch or Low German spansel, from spannen (“to bind, harness”).

parole.significato: To move quickly and nimbly on foot; to stride or run at a brisk pace.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Likely of Dutch or Low German origin. parole.significato: Speculoos, a spiced biscuit traditionally eaten around Saint Nicholas Day and Christmas; in particular, the variety fro…
parole.testo: From Dutch speculaas.

parole.significato: A type of spiced shortcrust biscuit.
parole.testo: From Dutch speculoos, Flemish form of speculaas.

parole.significato: A spiced Indonesian layer cake.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch spekkoek, literally “bacon cake”, since its dark and light layers are thought to resemble streaky bacon.

parole.significato: To split.
parole.testo: From Dutch or Middle Low German spletten, obscurely related to split and spleet.

parole.significato: A person or character like a Star Trek Vulcan; someone resembling Star Trek's character Spock.
parole.testo: Anglicized from Dutch Spaak.

parole.significato: A ghost or phantom.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch spook (“ghost”), from Middle Dutch spooc (“spook, ghost”). Cognate with Middle Low German spôk, spûk (“apparition, ghost”), Middle High German gespük (“a haunting”), German Spuk, Danish spøge (“to haunt”), Swedish spöke (“ghost”).

parole.significato: A tropical disease causing a sore throat and tongue, and disturbed digestion; psilosis.
parole.testo: From Dutch spruw, sprouw. First described by William Hillary.

parole.significato: A chief town in an area or country.
parole.testo: From Dutch stad. Doublet of stead.

parole.significato: The chief provincial magistrate, military commander, and, as a member of the House of Orange, highest-ranking noble in…
parole.testo: Partial calque of Dutch stadthouder (superseded), stadhouder (literally “placeholder”), from Middle Dutch stathouder, itself a calque of Medieval Latin locum tenēns. Doublet of locum tenens and lieutenant.

parole.significato: A town hall in a Dutch-speaking country or (former) colony.
parole.testo: Dutch stadhuis.

parole.significato: A traditional Dutch dish of potatoes mashed with one or more other vegetables, sometimes also with bacon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch stamppot, meaning "mash pot".

parole.significato: A transportable balance with unequal arm lengths.
parole.testo: From steel + yard (“enclosed area, rod”). The sense of “place” is a calque of Dutch staalhof or Middle Low German Stalhof (Modern Dutch staal (“steel”) + hof (“court, yard”)). parole.significato: A site or position (especially at shoreline or with reference to (former) Dutch colonies)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch stelling.

parole.significato: A work of art depicting an arrangement of inanimate objects.
parole.testo: Calque of Dutch stilleven.

parole.significato: A rack or pallet used to hold goods (originally casks) off the floor
parole.testo: From Dutch stellage.

parole.significato: The use of small dots that give the appearance of shading; the dots thus used.
parole.testo: Probably from Dutch stippel (“small dot”), originally applied to the dots themselves and later to the technique.

parole.significato: A small Dutch coin worth one twentieth of a guilder.
parole.testo: From Dutch stuiver, cognate with Middle Low German stüver.

parole.significato: To feed, stir up, especially, a fire or furnace.
parole.testo: From a back-formation of stoker, apparently from Dutch stoker, from stoken (“to kindle a fire, incite, instigate”), from Middle Dutch stoken (“to poke, thrust”), from stock (“stick, stock”), see: tandenstoker. Ultimately the same word as above.

parole.significato: The aperture through which a furnace is fed or tended.
parole.testo: From stoke + hole, after Dutch stookgat.

parole.significato: The staircase and landing or porch leading to the entrance of a residence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch stoep (“platform", "pavement”). Doublet of stoep. Cognate with step.

parole.significato: A Dutch waffle made from two thin wafers with syrup in between.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch stroopwafel, from stroop (“syrup”) + wafel (“wafer; waffle”).

parole.significato: stiver
parole.testo: From Dutch stuiver, from Middle Dutch stuyver, stuver (“a small coin”). Akin to Middle Low German stüver.

parole.significato: Unfermented grape juice; must.
parole.testo: From Dutch stom (“unfermented”, literally “mute; dull”). Compare French vin muet, German stummer Wein. Doublet of shtum.

parole.significato: Chicory (Cichorium intybus).
parole.testo: From earlier Dutch succoreye, sukereye (Modern Dutch suikerij (“chicory”)), from Middle Dutch, from Old French cicorée. Doublet of chicory.

parole.significato: A substance that has no resistance to conducting an electric current
parole.testo: From super- + conductor, calque of Dutch suprageleider (modern spelling supergeleider).

parole.significato: A person who follows an army, selling provisions.
parole.testo: From Dutch soeteler (modern zoetelaar).

parole.significato: Sweet mock orange (Philadelphus coronarius).
parole.testo: From Dutch or Middle Low German from Latin sȳrinx from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “pan pipes”).

parole.significato: A carved panel.
parole.testo: From Dutch tafereel (“panel, picture”), diminutive of tafel (“table”), from Latin tabula (“table”).

parole.significato: A large drinking vessel, sometimes of pewter, sometimes with a glass base, with one handle and often a hinged cover.
parole.testo: From Middle English tan(c)kard(e), denoting 'a large tub for carrying liquid', perhaps related to Dutch tanckaert, from Middle Dutch tanckaert, meaning the same thing, but of uncertain ultimate origin. parole.significato: A signal played five minutes before taps (lights out).
parole.testo: From earlier tap-to, borrowed from Dutch taptoe, from tap (“tap; faucet on a cask”) + toe (“to; shut”). More at tap, to.

parole.significato: The tea plant (Camellia sinensis); (countable) a variety of this plant.
parole.testo: First appears c. 1655, in the English translation Álvaro Semedo’s writings. From Dutch thee, from Hokkien 茶 (tê) (Amoy dialect), from Old Chinese, ultimately from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-la (“leaf, tea”). parole.testo: From Dutch terp (“terp”). See also thorp and thorpe.

parole.significato: Equivalent retribution; an act of returning exactly what one gets; an eye for an eye.
parole.testo: Uncertain; conjectured to be ultimately from Dutch dit voor dat (“this for that”) or French tant pour tant (“equal for equal”). parole.significato: An old Dutch sailing barge with a round bow, leeboards and a gaff-rigged mast.
parole.testo: From Dutch.

parole.significato: A shop in the Netherlands selling mainly Asian food products, and generally Asian- or Indo-European-owned.
parole.testo: From Dutch toko (“Southeast Asian grocery store”), from Malay toko (“shop”), from Hokkien 土庫 /土库 (thó͘-khò͘, “private storehouse”).

parole.significato: A brass alloy also known as red-bronze, usually containing 82-99% copper and the rest usually zinc.
parole.testo: From Dutch, from Malay tembaga (“copper”), from Sanskrit ताम्र (tāmra). Entered Dutch usage during colonial period. Doublet of tumbaga.

parole.significato: A pastry from the Netherlands resembling mille-feuille.
parole.testo: From Dutch tompoes, from French Tom Pouce, the French translation of English Tom Thumb.

parole.significato: A tactic in which the outfield players assume different roles during a game, while keeping an organised structure.
parole.testo: Calque of Dutch totaalvoetbal.

parole.significato: train oil, whale oil
parole.testo: From Dutch traan (“tear, drop”), from Middle Dutch trâen, from Old Dutch trān, from Proto-West Germanic *trahnu (“tear”). Compare German Träne (“tear”), Tran (“train oil”).

parole.significato: Oil obtained from the blubber of marine mammals, especially whale oil.
parole.testo: From train (“train oil”) + oil, partial calque of Dutch traanolie (“whale oil”). See further etymology at train.

parole.significato: A whitish, greyish volcanic tufa, formed of decomposed trachytic cinders, sometimes used as a cement.
parole.testo: From Dutch tras or German Trass, probably from Italian terrazzo (“terrace”). See terrace.

parole.significato: A net or dragnet used for trawling.
parole.testo: 16th century, borrowed from Dutch tragelen (“to pull with a towline, trawl”), from Middle Dutch traghelen, from traghel (“dragnet”) (presumably from Latin tragula (“dragnet”)), and as such root-cognate with English drag and dray.

parole.significato: A horse-drawn canal boat or riverboat, used to carry goods or passengers in the Netherlands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch trekschuit, from trekken (“pull”) + schuit (“boat”).

parole.significato: A trigger.
parole.testo: From Dutch trekker.

parole.significato: A finger-operated lever used to fire a gun.
parole.testo: Originally tricker, from Dutch trekker (“pull”, noun, as in drawer-pull, bell-pull), from Dutch trekken (“to drag, draw, pull”).

parole.significato: A kind of painting that depicts an exaggerated or characteristic facial expression.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch tronie.

parole.significato: A part of a person’s name (usually of Dutch origin) that comes between the first name and the last name.
parole.testo: From Dutch tussenvoegsel.

parole.significato: In motion, in progress; being done or carried out; on a journey.
parole.testo: Calque of Dutch onderweg (“underway”), equivalent to under- + way. Compare also German unterwegs.

parole.significato: Tumultuous, noisy excitement.
parole.testo: Calque of Dutch oproer or German Aufruhr, as up + roar.

parole.significato: After the fashion of; a la.
parole.testo: From Dutch op zijn.

parole.significato: The relatively weak attraction between neutral atoms and molecules arising from polarization induced in each particle b…
parole.testo: From van der Waals + force. From Dutch van der Waals. from Johannes Diderik van der Waals, who first described them.

parole.significato: A line extended down from the end of a gaff to regulate its position.
